<reflection>
The first experiment resulted in highly similar NLL values for most models (around -23.8), indicating that the conditions ([S]0=2.0, [cat]0=0.05, [P]0=0.2) did not sufficiently differentiate the mechanisms. Models M4 and M5 are effectively ruled out due to high NLLs. M6 and M8 have slightly better scores, suggesting a possible activation phase, but the evidence is weak. The models are currently degenerate, likely because the turnover number was moderate and the reaction trajectory didn't strongly penalize or reward specific deactivation or higher-order catalyst pathways. My aim to broadly separate the mechanisms was only partially achieved, as we need more extreme kinetic regimes to break this degeneracy.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
To break the degeneracy, especially between stable catalyst models (M1, M6, M8), substrate/product deactivation models (M11, M12, M14, M16, M17), and substrate inhibition (M7), I propose an experiment with a very high substrate-to-catalyst ratio. By setting a high initial substrate concentration ([S]0 = 5.0) and a low catalyst concentration ([cat]0 = 0.01) with no initial product ([P]0 = 0.0), we force the catalyst to undergo a large number of turnovers (500 turnovers required for full conversion).
1. Deactivation models will be clearly distinguished from stable models because the catalyst will deactivate before full conversion, leaving a plateau of unreacted substrate.
2. High [S]0 will saturate the catalyst, shifting the resting state to `catS`. This will amplify `catS`-mediated deactivation (M14, M16, M18) while suppressing free `cat`-mediated deactivation (M9, M13).
3. Substrate inhibition (M7) will be strongly triggered, resulting in an initially suppressed rate that accelerates as substrate is consumed.
4. Activation models (M6, M8) may reveal a distinct lag phase in product formation compared to the standard Michaelis-Menten (M1).
</hypothesis>
